name.text: Constraints and objective from a table

questiontext.text:
{@E[1]@} The table shows what each item needs, what is available, and the profit on each item. Let \(x\) be the number of {@E[2]@} and \(y\) the number of {@E[3]@}.

ResourceOne of the {@E[2]@} (\(x\))One of the {@E[3]@} (\(y\))Available
{@r1@}{@a1@}{@b1@}{@c1@}
{@r2@}{@a2@}{@b2@}{@c2@}
Profit (Ksh){@p1@}{@p2@}

(a) Write the inequality for the first resource, {@r1@}.

[[input:ans1]] [[validation:ans1]] [[feedback:prt1]]

(b) Write the inequality for the second resource, {@r2@}.

[[input:ans2]] [[validation:ans2]] [[feedback:prt2]]

(c) Write the profit \(P\), in Ksh, in terms of \(x\) and \(y\).

\(P =\) [[input:ans3]] [[validation:ans3]] [[feedback:prt3]]

(d) Can they make \({@x0@}\) {@E[2]@} and \({@y0@}\) {@E[3]@}?

[[input:ans4]] [[validation:ans4]] [[feedback:prt4]]

generalfeedback.text:
Each row of the table is one resource and gives one constraint: multiply each number by its letter, add, and compare with the amount available.

(a) \({@ta1@}\)

(b) \({@ta2@}\)

(c) \(P = {@ta3@}\). The profit is the objective function: it is not a constraint.

(d) Put \(x = {@x0@}\), \(y = {@y0@}\) into each inequality. First resource: \({@a1@} \times {@x0@} + {@b1@} \times {@y0@} = {@u1@}\), {@lt1@} the \({@c1@}\) available. Second resource: \({@a2@} \times {@x0@} + {@b2@} \times {@y0@} = {@u2@}\), {@lt2@} the \({@c2@}\) available. So the answer is: {@optd(keyp)@}

questiondescription.text:
Linear Programming: constraints and the objective function from a table

Grade 12 CBE Core 1.4 (a) / Essential 1.4 (a): Write one constraint for each row of a resource table, write the profit as an objective function, and check whether a plan is possible.

Core and Essential

This question is adapted from Chapter 8, Section 2.3, Example 2 of School Mathematics Project, SMP Book 5 (Metric), ed. P. G. Bowie, Cambridge University Press, 1969: a table of resources by product read into one constraint per resource, with the table transposed, an objective function and a plan check added, and Kenyan contexts and new numbers.

INNODEMS CBC Grade 12 Mathematics, first draft by Ben Davies, 2026. Aligned to the KICD Senior School Curriculum Design, Core and Essential Mathematics Grade 12 (draft).

truefeedback.text: You read down a column of the table: \({@a1@}\) and \({@a2@}\) are both amounts for one of the {@E[2]@}. Each row is one resource, so use the two numbers in the {@r1@} row, each with its letter.
You matched the numbers to the wrong letters: \(x\) counts the {@E[2]@}, so its number is in the {@E[2]@} column.
Your inequality says the amount used is \({@c1@}\) or more. The amount available is the most they can use.

falsefeedback.text: In the {@r1@} row, multiply each number by its letter, add, and compare with the amount available.

feedbackvariables.text: u10: subst([x = 1, y = 0], ans3); u01: subst([x = 0, y = 1], ans3);

truefeedback.text: The profits are matched to the wrong letters: \(x\) counts the {@E[2]@}, which make Ksh \({@p1@}\) each.
\(P\) depends on how many of each are made: multiply each profit by its letter.

falsefeedback.text: Test your expression with simple plans. For \(x = 1\), \(y = 0\) it gives \({@u10@}\), and for \(x = 0\), \(y = 1\) it gives \({@u01@}\). Compare these with the profit on one of the {@E[2]@} and on one of the {@E[3]@} in the table.

[[if test='is(ans4="yes")']]

Test the plan in each row of the table: work out \({@a1@} \times {@x0@} + {@b1@} \times {@y0@}\) for {@r1@} and \({@a2@} \times {@x0@} + {@b2@} \times {@y0@}\) for {@r2@}, and compare each total with the amount available.

[[/if]][[if test='is(ans4="n1")']][[if test='is(u1<=c1)']]

{@r1@}: \({@a1@} \times {@x0@} + {@b1@} \times {@y0@} = {@u1@}\), and \({@c1@}\) are available, so there is enough of this resource. Now test {@r2@} in the same way.

[[else]]

You are right that there is not enough for {@r1@}. Test {@r2@} too: compare \({@a2@} \times {@x0@} + {@b2@} \times {@y0@}\) with the \({@c2@}\) available.

[[/if]][[/if]][[if test='is(ans4="n2")']][[if test='is(u2<=c2)']]

{@r2@}: \({@a2@} \times {@x0@} + {@b2@} \times {@y0@} = {@u2@}\), and \({@c2@}\) are available, so there is enough of this resource. Now test {@r1@} in the same way.

[[else]]

You are right that there is not enough for {@r2@}. Test {@r1@} too: compare \({@a1@} \times {@x0@} + {@b1@} \times {@y0@}\) with the \({@c1@}\) available.

[[/if]][[/if]][[if test='is(ans4="nb")']][[if test='is(u1<=c1)']]

{@r1@}: \({@a1@} \times {@x0@} + {@b1@} \times {@y0@} = {@u1@}\), and \({@c1@}\) are available, so there is enough of this resource. So it is not both. Check {@r2@} again.

[[else]]

{@r2@}: \({@a2@} \times {@x0@} + {@b2@} \times {@y0@} = {@u2@}\), and \({@c2@}\) are available, so there is enough of this resource. So it is not both.

[[/if]][[/if]]
